Using members from dependent bases

MSVC allows unqualified lookup of members from dependent base classes in class templates, which is not permitted by the C++ standard. The standard requires two-phase lookup: dependent names must be explicitly qualified (using this-> or the base class name) because they cannot be resolved until template instantiation.

Noncompliant code example

template <typename T> struct Base { void baseMethod(); };

template <typename T> struct Derived : Base<T> {
  void method() {
    baseMethod(); // Noncompliant
  }
};

Compliant solution

template <typename T> struct Base { void baseMethod(); };

template <typename T> struct Derived : Base<T> {
  void method() {
    this->baseMethod(); // Or Base<T>::baseMethod();
  }
};

Related rules

  • S8216 - Code should not rely on features beyond the configured C++ standard
  • S3715 - GNU extensions should not be used
  • S8231 - Non-standard attributes should not be used
  • S4263 reports uses of MSVC-specific include file search strategy
  • S2260 tracks parsing failures and can help identify compiler-specific extensions that the analyzer fails to recognize
MSVC-specific extensions should not be used

name: Non-standard attributes should not be used

descriptionSections.content:
Attributes provide a standardized syntax for conveying implementation-defined language extensions and hints to the compiler. While the {C++} standard defines several attributes (such as [[deprecated]], [[maybe_unused]], and [[nodiscard]]), compilers also support vendor-specific attributes for compiler-specific features and optimizations.

Using non-standard attributes introduces portability risks. When code with compiler-specific attributes is compiled with a different toolchain, unrecognized attributes are silently ignored, which can lead to:

  • Loss of intended behavior (e.g., optimization hints, alignment requirements, or safety checks)
  • Runtime failures when the ignored attribute was critical for correctness
  • Maintenance burden when vendor-specific attributes are scattered across the codebase

This rule allows only standard attributes that are specified using the standard [[...]] syntax. It reports: * All attributes that are not defined in the {C++} standard itself, whether expressed using standard attribute syntax with vendor namespaces (e.g., [[msvc::no_unique_address]]), GNU-style __attribute__ syntax (e.g., __attribute__((packed))), or MSVC’s __declspec syntax (e.g., __declspec(align(16))) * Standard attributes that are specified using non-standard syntax (e.g., __attribute__((noreturn)) instead of [[noreturn]])

The goal is to ensure that such attributes are reviewed to be well-behaved under all used toolchains, or replaced with standard-conforming alternatives when possible.
Non-standard attributes should not be used

Related rules

  • S8216 - Code should not rely on features beyond the configured {C++} standard
  • S8230 - MSVC-specific extensions should not be used

Replace non-standard attributes with standard attributes when equivalent functionality exists, or ensure that vendor-specific attributes are only used in code paths that are known to be compiled with the appropriate toolchain. Consider using preprocessor directives or build-system configuration to conditionally apply compiler-specific attributes.

Non-standard attribute using standard syntax

Noncompliant code example

struct Empty {};

struct Container {
  [[msvc::no_unique_address]] Empty e; // Noncompliant: non-standard attribute
  int value;
};

Compliant solution

struct Empty {};

struct Container {
  [[no_unique_address]] Empty e; // Use standard attribute if C++20 is available
  int value;
};

Standard attribute using non-standard syntax

Noncompliant code example

__attribute__((noreturn))
void terminate(); // Noncompliant: standard attribute using GNU-style syntax

Compliant solution

[[noreturn]]
void terminate(); // Use standard syntax

name: Atomic operations should use sequential consistency

descriptionSections.content: Atomic operations should use sequential consistency (memory_order_seq_cst) to ensure predictable behavior.

Documentation

  • C++ reference - Memory ordering
  • C++ reference - std::atomic<T>

Articles & blog posts

  • Jeff Preshing - An Introduction to Lock-Free Programming

Replace weak memory orderings with memory_order::seq_cst, or simply omit the memory ordering parameter entirely since memory_order::seq_cst is the default for most atomic operations.

When you’re ready to optimize for performance, consider whether the complexity and architecture-specific behavior of weak orderings is worth the potential performance gain. In most cases, the performance difference is negligible compared to the maintenance cost and risk of subtle bugs.

Noncompliant code example

#include <atomic>

class Counter {
    std::atomic<int> count{0};
    std::atomic<bool> ready{false};

public:
    void decrement() {
        count.fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order::release); // Noncompliant: weak ordering
    }

    bool isReady() {
        return ready.load(std::memory_order::relaxed); // Noncompliant: weak ordering
    }

    void markReady() {
        ready.store(true, std::memory_order::relaxed); // Noncompliant: weak ordering
    }
};

Compliant solution

#include <atomic>

class Counter {
    std::atomic<int> count{0};
    std::atomic<bool> ready{false};

public:
    void decrement() {
        count.fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order::seq_cst); // Compliant: sequential consistency
        // Or simply: count.fetch_sub(1); // seq_cst is the default
        // Or simply: count--; // seq_cst is the default
    }

    bool isReady() {
        return ready.load(std::memory_order::seq_cst); // Compliant: sequential consistency
        // Or simply: return ready.load(); // seq_cst is the default
        // Or simply: return ready; // seq_cst is the default
    }

    void markReady() {
        ready.store(true, std::memory_order::seq_cst); // Compliant: sequential consistency
        // Or simply: ready.store(true); // seq_cst is the default
        // Or simply: ready = true; // seq_cst is the default
    }
};

How does this work?

Sequential consistency (memory_order::seq_cst) ensures that:

  1. All atomic operations appear to execute in a single, total order - imagine all threads agreeing on a timeline of when each operation happened
  2. No memory reordering occurs around atomic operations - the processor can’t move other memory accesses past atomic boundaries
  3. Behavior is identical across all processor architectures - your code works the same way on Intel, ARM, and other platforms

This makes reasoning about your program much simpler: if thread A stores a value and thread B loads it, you can be confident about what other memory operations thread B will observe.

Pitfalls

Even with this rule, keep in mind:

  • Sequential consistency doesn’t eliminate all race conditions - you still need proper synchronization design
  • Performance impact is usually minimal - modern processors are quite efficient with sequential consistency
  • Don’t mix memory orderings without expertise - if you use memory_order::seq_cst in some places and weaker orderings elsewhere, you reintroduce the complexity this rule aims to avoid
  • Atomic does not always mean lock-free - some atomic operations may still involve locks internally, so understand the performance characteristics of your specific atomic types
  • Reasoning with atomics is still complex - even with sequential consistency, concurrent programming requires careful design and testing; using mutexes or higher-level concurrency primitives is often a safer choice for complex synchronization needs

Going the extra mile

If you genuinely need the performance benefits of weak memory orderings:

  1. Profile first - measure whether memory ordering is actually a bottleneck
  2. Learn the memory model deeply - understand acquire/release semantics and their implications
  3. Use validation tools - tools can instrument the code to facilitate detecting and reproducing race conditions in atomic-based code
  4. Test on all target architectures - especially if they support relaxed memory models
  5. Document your reasoning - future maintainers will thank you

Atomic operations are special memory operations that appear to happen instantaneously and cannot be interrupted by other threads. They’re essential for safe communication between threads without using locks.

When working with atomic operations in C++, you can specify different memory ordering constraints that control how memory accesses are synchronized between threads.

Different memory orderings exist because modern processors use many optimization techniques to achieve high performance: they execute instructions out of order, reorder memory accesses, cache data at multiple levels, and predict branch outcomes, all of that happening simultaneously in different processors. These optimizations can make individual operations appear to happen in a different order than written in your code.

Memory models define the contract between hardware and software about which reorderings are acceptable. Stronger memory models provide more guarantees about ordering but may limit the processor’s ability to optimize. Weaker memory models allow more aggressive optimizations but require programmers to be more careful about synchronization.

The most common memory orderings are:

  • memory_order::seq_cst (sequential consistency) - The safest option that ensures all threads see operations in the same order, limiting some processor optimizations
  • memory_order::relaxed - The most permissive option that allows maximum reordering and optimization for performance
  • memory_order::acquire, memory_order::release - Intermediate options for specific synchronization patterns

While weaker memory orderings like memory_order::relaxed can offer performance benefits, they introduce significant complexity that makes concurrent code much harder to reason about correctly. The subtle semantics of these orderings are easy to misunderstand, leading to race conditions and unpredictable program behavior.

The main issues with weak memory orderings include:

  • Complex semantics - Understanding when and how memory operations can be reordered requires deep expertise
  • Subtle bugs - Race conditions may only manifest under specific timing or load conditions
  • Maintenance burden - Future code changes can inadvertently break the carefully crafted synchronization logic
  • Testing difficulties - Bugs may not appear consistently, making them hard to catch in development

Additionally, processor architecture differences compound these problems. For instance, Intel x86 processors use a relatively strong memory model ("Total Store Order"), so code with weak orderings executes in these environments as if they had stronger ordering. When the code, that has worked correctly for a very long time, is ported on processors with a more relaxed memory model that allows aggressive reordering, such as ARM, it may start to break in unexpected ways.

Using memory_order::seq_cst as the default choice eliminates these complexities by providing predictable, consistent behavior that’s much easier to understand and maintain.

This rule raises an issue when atomic operations explicitly use any std::memory_order enumerator other than seq_cst. This includes relaxed, consume, acquire, release, and acq_rel in atomic operations such as load(), store(), exchange(), compare_exchange_weak(), etc. Additionally, the rule flags cases where a non-constant value is assigned to a memory_order variable and then used in atomic operations, since the analyzer cannot determine at compile time whether the value will be memory_order::seq_cst or a weaker ordering. This pattern is also generally not meaningful, as memory ordering requirements are typically a compile-time design decision rather than a runtime parameter.

Atomic operations without an explicit memory ordering parameter use memory_order::seq_cst by default and are compliant with this rule.

What is the potential impact?

Using weak memory orderings inappropriately can lead to:

  • Race conditions that appear only on certain processor architectures
  • Data corruption due to unexpected memory access reordering
  • Inconsistent program behavior between development and production environments
  • Debugging nightmares where bugs are architecture-specific and hard to reproduce

name: Synchronization objects shall not have thread storage duration

descriptionSections.content:
Synchronization primitives — mutexes, condition variables, semaphores, latches, and barriers — are designed to coordinate access or execution across multiple threads. Their correctness depends on all participating threads operating on the same shared instance.

When a synchronization object is declared thread_local, the runtime creates a separate copy for each thread. Each thread then interacts only with its own copy, with no effect on any other thread.

This bug is particularly deceptive because the synchronization API is used correctly — the code compiles and runs without errors — but provides no actual synchronization.

Documentation

  • C++ reference - thread_local
  • C++ reference - std::mutex
  • C++ reference - std::condition_variable
  • C++ reference - std::counting_semaphore
  • C++ reference - std::latch
  • C++ reference - std::barrier

Move the synchronization object to a scope that is shared by all threads that need to synchronize: a non-local variable, a class data member, or a parameter passed by reference.

Noncompliant code example

#include <mutex>

thread_local std::mutex m; // Noncompliant
int sharedData = 0;

void increment() {
  std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m); // Each thread locks its own mutex
  ++sharedData;                        // No actual mutual exclusion
}

Compliant solution

#include <mutex>

std::mutex m; // Compliant: one instance shared across all threads
int sharedData = 0;

void increment() {
  std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
  ++sharedData;
}
Declaring a synchronization object with thread_local storage duration gives each thread its own independent copy, making the object useless for cross-thread coordination.

name: Mutex types shall not be directly dynamically allocated

descriptionSections.content:
Dynamically allocating a mutex gives the code explicit control over the mutex’s lifetime through pointer operations. This is problematic for two reasons.

First, destroying a locked mutex is undefined behavior. When a mutex is managed through a pointer, the code that destroys it (e.g., via delete) may not know whether any thread currently holds the lock. In contrast, a mutex with automatic or member storage duration is destroyed when its enclosing scope or object is destroyed. At this point, when proper techniques are consistently used, the mutex is guaranteed to be unlocked.

Second, a mutex should have the same lifetime as the data it protects. Dynamic allocation decouples the mutex lifetime from the data lifetime, making the code harder to reason about and increasing the risk of accessing data without the intended synchronization.

Instead, mutexes should be declared as data members of the class that owns the data they protect, or as local variables with the appropriate scope.

This rule raises an issue when one of the standard mutex types (std::mutex, std::timed_mutex, std::recursive_mutex, std::recursive_timed_mutex, std::shared_mutex, std::shared_timed_mutex) is dynamically allocated using new, std::make_unique, or std::make_shared.

Documentation

  • C++ reference - std::mutex

Declare the mutex as a data member of the class that owns the data it protects, or as a local variable with appropriate scope.

In the simplest case, a mutex used to protect a local critical section should be declared as a local variable, not heap-allocated:

Noncompliant code example

void doSomethingCritical() {
  std::mutex* mut = new std::mutex; // Noncompliant
  int value = 0;
  auto workerThread = spawnWorkerThread(mut, &value);
  std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(*mut);
  ++value;
  workerThread.join(); // Not necessary when using jthread
  delete mut; // Undefined behavior: mut is still locked
}

Compliant solution

void doSomethingCritical() {
  std::mutex mut; // Compliant: destroyed after guard, which unlocks it first
  int value = 0;
  auto workerThread = spawnWorkerThread(&mut, &value);
  std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(mut);
  ++value;
  workerThread.join(); // Not necessary when using jthread
}

When a mutex and the data it protects are allocated separately, their lifetimes are not coupled, which makes it easy to destroy one without the other:

Noncompliant code example

std::mutex* mtx = new std::mutex;   // Noncompliant
int* value = new int(0);

void increment() {
  std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(*mtx);
  ++(*value);
}

Compliant solution

struct SharedData {
  std::mutex mtx;
  int value = 0;
};

auto data = std::make_unique<SharedData>(); // Compliant: mutex and data share lifetime

void increment() {
  std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(data->mtx);
  ++data->value;
}
